blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Typed decision models (TDMs) return a probability over caller-defined options, and Jev is described by its vendor as calibrated. But in deployment class frequencies change, so calibration measured on a fixed test set need not hold where thresholds are applied. Existing evaluations leave two gaps: the gains of vendor decision training have not been separated from those of the backbone under an identical readout, and TDMs have been tested only at the test set's class distribution. We ask whether decision training improves a model over its own backbone, and whether a TDM's calibration and thresholds withstand prevalence (label) shift as well as a fine-tuned classifier's. We compare three TDMs (Jev, Tev1-4B, Nimble-9B), their base models and two trained classifiers on identical decisions from five public datasets under simulated shift, with 35 paired tests fixed before any test was computed. First, decision training is not uniformly beneficial: Nimble-9B, which differs from Qwen3.5-9B only by a LoRA adapter, is better calibrated on intent tasks but 12.0 Macro-F1 points worse on financial sentiment. Second, under moderate shift Jev's expected calibration error (ECE) and threshold risk grow significantly more than a fine-tuned DeBERTa's only on financial sentiment, by 1.7 and 2.5 percentage points; averaged over 2,000 shift scenarios (exploratory), the gap is at most one point on every dataset. Third, EM prior correction with the model's mean development prediction as its prior needs no labels and lowers Jev's ECE under shift by 2.7 and 1.8 points on the two datasets where it is highest, although labelled recalibration lowers it far more. The three TDMs we tested are neither uniformly better than their backbones nor uniquely fragile under shift; for calibration, their main weakness is the miscalibration they already have without shift. We release all inputs, code and outputs.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Consider a bank that routes incoming customer messages to one of a fixed set of intents and sends a message to a
human whenever the routing model is less than 90% confident. The threshold was chosen on validation data in which,
say, one message in ten was a complaint. After a service outage, four messages in ten are complaints. The model,
the messages of each kind and the threshold are unchanged; only the class frequencies have moved. Does the model’s
confidence still mean what it meant at validation time, and does the threshold still send the intended share of
messages to a human?

blocks.en:
This question has become practical for a new class of models. Typed decision models (TDMs), also called
“System One” models, do not generate text: given an input and a caller-defined set of options, they return a
probability distribution over the options ( Deußer et al., 2026 ; Tang & Zheng, 2026 ) . Jev is offered as a hosted API and
is described by its vendor as calibrated; Tev1-4B and Nimble-9B are open models fine-tuned from Qwen3.5 backbones
for the same interface. A trained classifier has a training prior that label-shift corrections can use ( Saerens et al., 2002 ; Lipton et al., 2018 ) . A zero-shot model has none. The closest substitute is an implicit prior : the average distribution the model predicts on a development set, which requires no labels.

blocks.en:
Existing evaluations leave two gaps. First, the benefit of vendor “decision training” has not been separated from the
backbone: an audit of early TDM papers calls for same-backbone ablations ( Tang & Zheng, 2026 ) , existing comparisons of
a vendor TDM with its backbone read the two models out differently ( Rafe & Das, 2026 ) , and the study that does
compare identical weights fine-tunes its own models and finds gains only on some tasks ( Li & Wagle, 2026 ) . Second, TDMs have been compared with language models and trained classifiers at a
single class distribution ( Deußer et al., 2026 ; Rafe & Das, 2026 ) , so it is not known whether their calibration and
thresholds transfer when the class frequencies change; a recent audit of 28 TDM papers lists calibration under
deployment shift as an open problem ( Tang & Zheng, 2026 ) . Prior adaptation without labels has been studied for language
models and vision–language models ( Estienne, 2023 ; Han et al., 2026 ) , but not for TDMs against trained
classifiers under controlled shift. We are not aware of a study that combines a commercial TDM, open TDMs paired with
their own backbones, trained classifiers and controlled prevalence shift with label-free prior correction
( Table 1 ); this combination is what allows us to ask what decision training adds and whether it
survives a change in class frequencies.

blocks.en:
We study three research questions on five public, human-labelled datasets, using identical test items and
candidate sets for every system: RQ1 (decision training): does vendor decision training change accuracy and calibration relative to the same
backbone? RQ2 (prevalence shift): under controlled prevalence shift, do a TDM’s calibration error and threshold risk
change differently from those of a fine-tuned classifier? RQ3 (implicit-prior correction): does expectation–maximisation (EM) prior correction with the implicit
prior reduce a TDM’s calibration error under shift?
Our results concern candidate-set decisions, in which the gold label is always among 3–22 offered options, and simulated label shift, in which only the class frequencies change; they do not cover full-label classification
over all 150 or 64 intents, or deployment shifts that also change the text of each class ( Section 7 ).
The tests and the comparison family were fixed and hashed before the final runs, and the analysis before any test was
computed ( Section 4 ); the one amendment, and earlier exposures of test data
during pipeline checks (mainly the FPB test split), are listed in Appendix A .

blocks.en:
Our findings are as follows ( Figure 1 ; all 35 tests in Table 7 ). • Decision training is task-dependent. Nimble-9B, which differs from Qwen3.5-9B only by a LoRA
adapter, is better calibrated on both intent datasets but 12.0 Macro-F1 points worse on financial sentiment, where
its calibration error is also higher ( Section 5.1 ). Tev1-4B is never significantly worse than
Qwen3.5-4B, and is better on five of ten tests. • Moderate prevalence shift separates Jev from a fine-tuned classifier only a little. At a Dirichlet
concentration of α = 1 \alpha=1 , Jev’s ECE and the excess risk of its confidence threshold grow significantly
more than DeBERTa-v3-large’s (after Holm correction) only on FPB, by 1.7 and 2.5 percentage points; averaged over
2,000 shift scenarios (exploratory), the difference is at most one point on every dataset and largest on TREC-6 ( Section 5.2 ). • Implicit-prior correction helps where calibration is poor. EM with Jev’s implicit prior, which needs
no labels, lowers Jev’s ECE under shift by 2.7 points on FPB and 1.8 points on HateXplain, the two datasets where its
unshifted ECE is highest (0.095 and 0.279), with the same sign for every prior set; on the other three datasets the
effect is not significant after Holm correction. Recalibration on labelled development data lowers the error much
further ( Section 5.3 ). • Artifacts. We release the frozen label texts, candidate sets, prompts, evaluation code and every
per-example probability vector at https://github.com/AbdulRahmanIqbal/tdm-prevalence-shift . In short, decision training helps a backbone on some tasks and hurts it on others, and prevalence shift matters less
for the TDMs we tested than the calibration error they already have without shift.

blocks.en:
Jev was released in September 2026, and evaluations followed within weeks. Deußer et al. (2026) evaluate Jev
zero-shot on 37 public datasets against two open models and report well-calibrated choice probabilities overall, with
miscalibration, mostly overconfidence, concentrated on the datasets where accuracy is low. Rafe & Das (2026) compare several TDMs with trained classifiers and generative models under matched conditions
and find that the ranking depends on whether task labels exist; they also compare each decoder-based TDM, including Nimble,
with its Qwen3.5 backbone, but read the backbone out differently (by option-key likelihood), on their typed-decision
benchmark, a sample of CLINC150 and several social-science tasks. Li & Wagle (2026) argue that general-purpose
language models already behave like Jev-style decision models when read out by scoring the candidate labels, and that
fine-tuning helps only on some tasks. Other early studies cover annotation tasks in computational social science ( Ibrahim & Zaki, 2026 ) , optimised natural-looking context that flips decisions ( Xu et al., 2026 ) , and
confidence-based escalation of LLM judges ( Li et al., 2026 ) . An audit of 28 early TDM papers finds no independent accuracy advantage of the typed readout over
comparable label-probability readouts, and lists calibration under deployment shift and the attribution of gains as
open problems ( Tang & Zheng, 2026 ) . All of these studies evaluate at the class distribution of the test set. Our
study varies the class distribution in a controlled way, and pairs each open TDM with its base model under the same
prompt, readout and precision, on five datasets; for Nimble-9B, which differs from its base only by an adapter, this
isolates the effect of decision training.

target prior with EM, using the classifier’s posteriors and the training prior. Black-box shift estimation ( Lipton et al., 2018 ) and its regularised variant ( Azizzadenesheli et al., 2019 ) estimate the target
prior from a confusion matrix. Alexandari et al. (2020) show that EM is hard to beat once the classifier is
calibrated with class-specific biases (BCTS), and Garg et al. (2020) unify these estimators and attribute the
advantage of maximum likelihood to calibration. All of these methods assume a known source prior. For zero-shot
models, which have no training prior, prior adaptation without labels has been proposed for language models ( Estienne, 2023 ) , and zero-shot CLIP models have been adapted to a given label-distribution prior ( Kahana et al., 2022 ) or to an unknown target distribution estimated from unlabelled test data ( Han et al., 2026 ) . We use the simplest
version of this idea, the mean predicted distribution on a development set as an implicit source prior, and test it
on a commercial TDM against a trained classifier whose source prior is known.

Modern networks are often miscalibrated, and temperature scaling on held-out data is a strong fix ( Guo et al., 2017 ) . Fine-tuned transformers are relatively well calibrated in-domain ( Desai & Durrett, 2020 ) ,
whereas prompted language models carry label biases that a content-free calibration step can reduce ( Zhao et al., 2021 ) . We measure calibration with top-label ECE and selective risk ( Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017 ) , and
ask how both change when the class frequencies move.

With enough labelled data, fine-tuned encoders tend to outperform in-context or zero-shot use of larger language models
on text classification ( Edwards & Camacho-Collados, 2024 ; Bucher & Martini, 2024 ) . Fine-tuning on few examples is, however, unstable ( Mosbach et al., 2021 ; Zhang et al., 2021 ) , which our
training protocol takes into account. We compare against classifiers trained on the full training sets, the setting in
which a trained classifier is strongest.

blocks.en:
We use five public, human-labelled English datasets that represent common decision tasks
( Table 2 ): intent classification for assistants, CLINC150 in-scope ( Larson et al., 2019 ) and
HWU64 ( Liu et al., 2021 ) ; financial sentiment, FPB ( Malo et al., 2014 ) ; hate and offensive speech,
HateXplain ( Mathew et al., 2021 ) ; and question type, TREC-6 ( Li & Roth, 2002 ) . CLINC150, HateXplain and
TREC-6 use their official splits. FPB has no official split; we use a public 64/16/20 split of the 50%-agreement subset,
following Araci (2019) , whose 970-example test set is the one used by Deußer et al. (2026) . For HWU64 and TREC-6, which have no official development
split, the development set is a stratified sample of the training set that follows the training class distribution.
Train and development texts that duplicate a test text after normalisation (lower-casing and removing punctuation),
and texts that occur with conflicting labels, are removed; the test sets are never changed. All raw files and processed
splits are pinned by SHA-256 hashes.

blocks.zh: 5 结果

blocks.en:
All 16,234 Jev calls and all local predictions returned a valid probability vector: no request failed after retries
and no input was refused, including on HateXplain. On the 970-example FPB test set that Deußer et al. (2026) also use,
Jev’s accuracy is 0.744, consistent with the 0.730 they report. Full-data DeBERTa-v3-large reaches 0.976 accuracy on
TREC-6, close to the 0.974 reported for fully fine-tuned RoBERTa-large ( Gao et al., 2021 ) , and 0.703 Macro-F1 on
HateXplain, slightly above the best value we found reported for that test split, 0.699 ( Kim et al., 2022 ) . The four local
models gave identical probabilities when 50 CLINC150 development examples were scored twice. Jev is not: in four runs over the same 500 test examples per dataset, it returned the same
prediction for 96.4–99.8% of examples but the same probability vector for only 19.4–87.4% of them, with differences of
up to 0.29 between runs; its ECE on these subsets varied by at most 0.012 between runs ( Appendix B ). All
analyses use a single full run of each system.

Because these confirmatory estimates are conditional on one set of target priors, we repeated PA1–PA3 with five other
prior sets (exploratory, added after the results were known; Table 5 ). On FPB, Jev’s ECE change exceeds
DeBERTa-v3-large’s for every prior set, but by 0.3 to 1.7 points (the frozen set is among the largest), and its excess

direction depends on the prior set: the frozen set favours Jev ( − 0.8 -0.8 ), the five others favour DeBERTa-v3-large ( + 0.2 +0.2 to + 0.8 +0.8 ). Averaged over 2,000 target priors drawn at α = 1 \alpha=1 (exploratory; Table 14 ), the PA1
difference is + 0.4 +0.4 points on FPB, 0.0 0.0 on HateXplain and + 1.0 +1.0 on TREC-6, and at most 0.1 0.1 on the intent datasets;
on FPB and HateXplain the difference varies widely between single priors (standard deviation 5.4 and 7.4 points), so a
set of 50 priors is not enough to pin down its mean. PA3, in contrast, keeps its sign and remains clearly negative: − 1.7 -1.7 points on FPB (frozen set − 2.7 -2.7 ) and − 2.0 -2.0 on HateXplain (frozen set − 1.8 -1.8 ). We therefore read RQ2 as follows: under moderate shift, Jev’s calibration error grows by at most 1.7 points more than that of a fine-tuned classifier on any prior set, and by at most one point on average over shifts;
the direction is consistent on FPB and TREC-6, and the size of such differences depends on which shifts are considered. Two facts call for caution about the significant FPB results (PA1 and PA2). FPB is the
dataset whose test split was used in pipeline checks before the protocol was frozen ( Appendix A ),
and the size of the estimate is not stable across prior sets (0.3 to 1.7 points). Jev’s own run-to-run variation in ECE
on FPB, measured on repeated calls over 500 test examples, is at most 0.6 points ( Table 10 ), well below
the frozen estimate, so the non-determinism of the API is unlikely to explain the FPB result, whereas its size depends
strongly on the prior set. We therefore do not treat RQ2 as evidence that Jev is more fragile under shift than a trained classifier; the
robust conclusion is that the difference is small.

The arms fall into two categories that should not be compared as alternatives: EM with the implicit prior is label-free and is the only option when no labelled data are available, whereas temperature scaling and BCTS+EM
are labelled recalibration fitted on the labelled development set (the oracle uses the true target prior and is
only a reference). Figure 5 and Table 12 compare all five arms. On FPB and HateXplain, where most systems are
miscalibrated, bias-corrected temperature scaling followed by EM gives the lowest ECE under shift for 13 of the 14
system–dataset pairs, for example 0.035 for Nimble-9B on FPB against 0.271 without recalibration; the exception is
DeBERTa-v3-large on FPB, where temperature scaling alone is 0.2 points lower. Its gain is mostly the correction of
miscalibration that exists without shift: relative to its own no-shift control, the ECE of BCTS+EM still rises under shift,
by 1.5 to 3.1 points for the zero-shot systems on HateXplain, more than the raw probabilities do there, but it stays far
below the unrecalibrated level. Temperature scaling alone transfers less well: its ECE increases under shift more than

8 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 8 结论

blocks.en:
We compared typed decision models with their own backbones and with trained classifiers on identical items and
candidate sets, under controlled prevalence shift and with 35 tests fixed before any test was computed. Vendor decision
training changed the same backbone in a task-dependent direction: with only an adapter between them, Nimble-9B was better
calibrated than Qwen3.5-9B on intent tasks and 12 Macro-F1 points worse on financial sentiment (RQ1). Under moderate
prevalence shift, Jev’s calibration error and threshold risk grew significantly more than those of a fine-tuned DeBERTa
only on financial sentiment (by 1.7 and 2.5 points); this difference depended on the shift scenarios, and averaged over
many scenarios it was at most one point on every dataset (RQ2). A label-free EM correction with the model’s implicit
prior lowered Jev’s calibration error under shift by 2.7 and 1.8 points on the two datasets where it was highest,
consistently in sign across scenarios, but recalibration on labelled development data reduced it much further (RQ3).
The three typed decision models we tested are neither uniformly better than their backbones nor uniquely fragile under
prevalence shift; for calibration, their main weakness is the miscalibration they already have without shift. Whether
one is enough for a task is best decided by testing it against its base model and recalibrating it on labelled data
from the deployment setting.

blocks.en: Broader impact statement
blocks.zh: 更广泛的影响说明

blocks.en:
Typed decision models are built to make automated decisions inside software, for example routing, moderation and
triage. Our results show that their calibration and the error rate of confidence thresholds can change when the
deployment class distribution differs from the evaluation data, and that decision training can make a model worse on a
task. Deploying such models in consequential settings (moderation, finance, health) without validation on target data
can therefore cause harm; we recommend task-specific evaluation against a base model, recalibration on labelled data,
and monitoring of threshold error rates. HateXplain contains offensive text; we used it only for evaluation.

in the vendors’ documentation as training or evaluation data or as candidates for it. The later Nimble release
( main ) lists 500 public TREC questions in its training data, which is why the confirmatory pair uses the
